subject: Modern History
sub_topic: Women's organisations — All India Women's Conference

concepts.name: Founding and Origins of the All India Women's Conference (AIWC)
key_dimensions: Founded in 1927 by Margaret Cousins (Irish theosophist) — UPSC trap: often confused with Indian founders
Initial mandate was education reform for women, NOT political suffrage — evolution of scope over time
First session held in Pune (1927) — location and presiding figures
Distinction between AIWC's founding context vs. other women's bodies like Women's India Association (WIA, 1917)

concepts.name: Margaret Cousins and the Role of Non-Indian Founders in AIWC
key_dimensions: Margaret Cousins as co-founder — Irish suffragette and Theosophical Society connections
Intersection of Theosophy, Annie Besant's influence, and women's organizing in colonial India
Debate over indigenous vs. externally-inspired origins of Indian women's organizations
Comparison with Annie Besant's role in Home Rule League — foreign women in Indian nationalist causes

concepts.name: AIWC's Initial Focus: Women's Education and Reform vs. Political Emancipation
key_dimensions: Original mandate: improving women's education — schools, curricula, literacy campaigns
Gradual shift from social reform to political demands (suffrage, legal rights)
Internal tension between 'social uplift' faction and 'political rights' faction within AIWC
Comparison with National Council of Women in India (NCWI) — overlapping but distinct mandates

concepts.name: AIWC and the Demand for Women's Suffrage in Colonial India
key_dimensions: AIWC's role in lobbying for women's franchise before the Government of India Act, 1935
Sarojini Naidu's testimony to the Joint Select Committee on constitutional reforms
Limited vs. universal suffrage debate — property qualifications and literacy tests affecting women
Comparison: Women's suffrage achieved in provincial legislatures (1935) vs. universal adult franchise (1950 Constitution)

concepts.name: Key Leaders of AIWC and Their Distinct Contributions
key_dimensions: Sarojini Naidu — President of AIWC and INC; bridging nationalist and women's movements
Muthulakshmi Reddi — first woman legislator in India; championed abolition of devadasi system through AIWC
Rajkumari Amrit Kaur — long-serving Secretary; later India's first Health Minister
Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit — AIWC connection and international diplomacy; UPSC trap: her roles often conflated with Sarojini Naidu's

concepts.name: AIWC and Social Reform Legislation: Child Marriage, Widow Remarriage, and Devadasi Abolition
key_dimensions: AIWC's advocacy leading to the Sarda Act (Child Marriage Restraint Act, 1929) — minimum age provisions
Campaign against the devadasi system — Muthulakshmi Reddi's Devadasi Bill in Madras Legislature
AIWC's position on widow remarriage and property rights for Hindu women
UPSC trap: Sarda Act associated with Har Bilas Sarda, not directly with AIWC — but AIWC lobbied for it

concepts.name: AIWC's Relationship with the Indian National Congress
key_dimensions: AIWC maintained formal organizational independence from INC — unlike women's wings of political parties
Personal overlaps: many AIWC leaders were also INC members (Sarojini Naidu, Kamladevi Chattopadhyay)
AIWC's non-partisan stance vs. active participation of its members in civil disobedience movements
INC's Karachi Resolution (1931) — fundamental rights including equality of sexes; AIWC's influence on this

concepts.name: AIWC and the Civil Disobedience Movement (1930–34)
key_dimensions: AIWC members' participation in Salt Satyagraha — Kamladevi Chattopadhyay's symbolic salt purchase
Organizational tension: AIWC as a body did not officially endorse civil disobedience (non-partisan stance)
Individual AIWC leaders as mass mobilizers of women during the movement
Contrast with Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) — earlier phase of women's entry into nationalist politics

concepts.name: Kamladevi Chattopadhyay and AIWC's Radical Feminist Strand
key_dimensions: Kamladevi as AIWC president and her push for more overtly political and socialist feminism
Her role in linking women's rights to anti-colonial struggle and economic independence
Kamladevi vs. moderate social reform strand within AIWC — internal ideological spectrum
Her later contributions: revival of Indian handicrafts, cooperative movement — continuity of AIWC's broader vision

concepts.name: AIWC and Hindu Personal Law Reform: Towards the Hindu Code Bill
key_dimensions: AIWC's decades-long campaign for uniform civil code and Hindu personal law reform
Memoranda submitted to British government and later to Constituent Assembly demanding women's property rights
Connection to Hindu Code Bill debates (1948–56) — B.R. Ambedkar's bill and AIWC's support
UPSC trap: Hindu Code Bill was ultimately split into four acts (1955–56), not passed as a single code

concepts.name: AIWC and the Constituent Assembly: Women's Rights in the Constitution
key_dimensions: AIWC members as Constituent Assembly members — Rajkumari Amrit Kaur, Hansa Mehta, Durgabai Deshmukh
AIWC's influence on Article 14 (equality), Article 15 (non-discrimination), and Article 15(3) (special provisions for women)
Hansa Mehta's role in replacing 'all men are born equal' with 'all human beings' in UDHR — AIWC link
Debate over separate electorates for women — AIWC's position against communal/gender-based separate electorates

concepts.name: AIWC vs. Women's India Association (WIA) and National Council of Women in India (NCWI): Comparative Analysis
key_dimensions: WIA (1917, Madras) — Annie Besant, Margaret Cousins, Sarojini Naidu; focused on political rights first
NCWI (1925) — Mehribai Tata; affiliated to International Council of Women; elite philanthropic focus
AIWC (1927) — broadest pan-Indian reach; education-first but evolved to political demands
UPSC trap: WIA predates AIWC; Margaret Cousins was involved in both — chronology and membership overlaps

concepts.name: AIWC's Stance on Purdah, Zenana System, and Women's Mobility
key_dimensions: AIWC's explicit campaign against purdah as an impediment to women's education and civic participation
Differentiated approach: persuasion and awareness vs. legislative prohibition of purdah
Intersection with caste — purdah as upper-caste/upper-class practice; AIWC's class composition and its limitations
Comparison with Muslim women's organizations' approach to purdah reform — AIWC's cross-community outreach

concepts.name: AIWC and International Women's Movements: Transnational Connections
key_dimensions: AIWC's affiliation with International Alliance of Women (IAW) and participation in global suffrage campaigns
Hansa Mehta at the UN Commission on the Status of Women and UDHR drafting — AIWC's global projection
Influence of British suffragette movement on AIWC founders vs. Gandhian non-violent methodology
UPSC angle: India's early contribution to international gender equality norms through AIWC leaders

concepts.name: AIWC's Publications, Propaganda, and Awareness Campaigns
key_dimensions: AIWC's journal 'Roshni' (later 'The Indian Women') as a platform for feminist discourse
Use of conferences, pamphlets, and public meetings to reach literate middle-class women
Limitation: primarily urban, educated, upper/middle-class reach — rural and working-class women largely excluded
Contrast with Gandhi's mass mobilization model — AIWC's organizational approach vs. Gandhian grassroots method

concepts.name: AIWC and the Abolition of Child Marriage: Sarda Act (1929) and Its Aftermath
key_dimensions: AIWC's sustained lobbying campaign preceding the Child Marriage Restraint Act, 1929
Act's provisions: minimum age 14 for girls, 18 for boys (raised later) — UPSC trap: original vs. amended ages
Criticism of the Act: weak enforcement, no provision for annulment of child marriages
AIWC's continued advocacy post-1929 for stronger implementation — gap between legislation and social reality

concepts.name: AIWC's Role in the Quit India Movement (1942) and Wartime Nationalism
key_dimensions: Participation of AIWC members in underground activities during Quit India Movement despite organizational non-partisanship
Aruna Asaf Ali — though not exclusively an AIWC figure, represents the radical women's nationalist strand
AIWC's dilemma: organizational neutrality vs. members' nationalist commitment during wartime repression
Women's participation in parallel government (Tamluk/Satara) — grassroots women beyond AIWC's urban reach

concepts.name: Class, Caste, and Community Limitations of AIWC's Feminism
key_dimensions: AIWC's predominantly upper-caste Hindu, English-educated membership — 'elite feminism' critique
Limited engagement with Dalit women's issues — contrast with B.R. Ambedkar's women's rights agenda
Muslim women's representation in AIWC and tensions over personal law reform vs. communal identities
UPSC analytical angle: AIWC as representative of 'mainstream nationalism's women's wing' vs. marginalised women's movements

concepts.name: Post-Independence Continuity: AIWC's Role After 1947
key_dimensions: AIWC's transition from a freedom-struggle-era body to a post-independence women's welfare organization
Rajkumari Amrit Kaur as Health Minister — policy continuity from AIWC agenda to state policy
AIWC's role in advocating for the Hindu Code Bills (1955–56) and later the Dowry Prohibition Act (1961)
UPSC trap: AIWC is still functional today — its founding and its current status as a registered NGO are distinct

concepts.name: AIWC and the Devadasi Abolition Movement: Intersection of Gender, Caste, and Religion
key_dimensions: Muthulakshmi Reddi's campaign within AIWC to frame devadasi system as sexual exploitation, not religious tradition
Madras Devadasi (Prevention of Dedication) Act, 1947 — AIWC's role in achieving this legislation
Tension between AIWC's reform agenda and devadasi community's own agency and self-representation
UPSC comparative angle: devadasi abolition vs. temple entry movements (Vaikom Satyagraha) — different reform strategies
